entries.proposition: Delivery: rapamycin 40 ug/mL in the drinking water of lactating dams (vehicle 0.5 percent ethanol), pups treated through milk from P10 to P21; pup dose and exposure are not measured.
entries.snippet: Lactating females were provided drinking water with 40ug/ml of rapamycin (RAP) or 0.5% ethanol as a vehicle (VEH) to treat Npc1nmf164 mouse pups through maternal lactation from P10 to P21.
entries.anchor: Results / Rapamycin reduces proliferation and phagocytic activity

entries.proposition: There is no wild-type rapamycin arm and no vehicle-only wild-type arm of the same treatment, so the effect of rapamycin on normal development is not tested.
entries.snippet: Data are presented as mean ± SEM, n = 3-4 mice/group, *P < 0.05 and ***P < 0.001 by unpaired t-test (B-D) or One-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey (F-H).

entries.proposition: Rapamycin raised MBP volume in the cerebellar white matter of Npc1 mutant pups at P21 (the myelin endpoint).
entries.snippet: rapamycin treatment significantly increased MBP immunolabeling in the cerebellar WMR of Npc1nmf164 mice compared to vehicle-treated Npc1nmf164 mice at P21 (Fig 7A–B)

entries.proposition: The paper states white-matter microglia were unchanged by rapamycin, so the myelin effect is not attributed to the microglial arm.
entries.snippet: Yet, no differences in the total volume of IBA1+ microglia and the mean volume of CD68+ phagosomes were found between vehicle- and rapamycin-treated Npc1nmf164 mice (Fig 7A,C–D).

entries.proposition: Harm signal: rapamycin further shortened microglial processes and reduced terminal points in the molecular layer and increased process diameter, which the authors read as impaired postnatal microglial growth.
entries.snippet: However, rapamycin also impaired microglial processes development, underscoring mTORC1’s importance in postnatal microglial growth and differentiation.

entries.proposition: Rapamycin did not rescue the Tmem119-EGFP deficit (persistent immaturity of molecular-layer microglia).
entries.snippet: However, rapamycin treatment failed to rescue this phenotype, indicating that mTORC1 signaling does not directly regulate Tmem119 expression in this context.

entries.proposition: Rapamycin prevented loss of VGLUT2-positive climbing-fibre terminals in the molecular layer at P21; this is a synaptic, not an excitability, endpoint.
entries.snippet: We found that the significant decrease of VGLUT2+ in presynaptic terminals/axons observed in vehicle-treated Npc1nmf164 mice at P21 was prevented by rapamycin treatment when compared to wild-type mice (Fig 6A–B).

entries.proposition: The glial arm: microglia numbers and morphology are the gliosis readout; astrocytic GFAP is not measured anywhere in the paper.
entries.snippet: Using rapamycin to inhibit mTORC1 in Npc1nmf164 mice during postnatal development, we found the impact of this pathway in postnatal microglia and the developmental pathology associated with NPC1 deficiency in Npc1nmf164 mice.

entries.proposition: Group sizes are 3-4 mice; mixed sex; the authors say interpretation is by age and genotype alone.
entries.snippet: Although mixed-sex groups were used, due to limited sample sizes, all findings in this study were interpreted based on age and/or genotype differences alone.

entries.proposition: mTORC1 hyperactivation in P7 Npc1 microglia is absent: pS6 was lower than in wild type at P7 and rose only by P10, so the premise that mTORC1 is hyperactive from birth is not supported by the data.
entries.snippet: Interestingly, at this postnatal stage (P7), the mean fluorescence intensity of pS6R was significantly reduced in IBA1+ PAM cells within the dWMR of Npc1nmf164 mice compared to wild-type controls (Fig 4A and C).
